title: Finitely generated modules and finite modules over a finite ring
statement: Let $R$ be a ring and $M$ an $R$-module. $M$ is *finitely generated* (a *finite* $R$-module) if there are finitely many elements $m_1,\ldots,m_r\in M$ such that every element of $M$ is an $R$-linear combination $\sum_j a_jm_j$ with $a_j\in R$. When $R$ is a finite ring, an $R$-module is finitely generated if and only if its underlying set is finite; so for a finite ring $R$ a *finite $R$-module* means, without ambiguity, a finitely generated $R$-module, equivalently one with finitely many elements. When $R$ is a field, a finitely generated $R$-module is a finite-dimensional $R$-vector space [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace].

source.place: Stacks Project, Algebra, Section 'Finite modules and finitely presented modules' (Tag 0517), Definition 0518 (finite = finitely generated module); the equivalence over a finite ring is elementary (a finite set generates M; conversely M is a quotient of R^r, a finite set when R is finite)
